utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Mr. Stevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I just -- maybe this -- there may have been a miscommunications between the Prosecution and the Chambers, but we believe that we need the Rule 90 warning in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was not a miscommunication. It was my fault. Yes. Mr. Stevic, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic or the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer that question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Stevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stevic, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for pausing before answer, and make it even longer between my question and your answer and to speak slowly so that everything can be properly recorded so that we don't have interruptions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D7970 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this statement, and have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to the last page so that the witness can see his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told my Defence team.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I asked you today the same questions, would your answers essentially be the same as the ones given in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I think they would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this please be admitted into evidence under 92 ter Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering any associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read a brief summary of Mr. Vujadin Stevic's statement in English. [In English] Vujadin Stevic was born on 12th of May, 1958 in Ljubovija, Serbia, and currently resides in Slapasnica in Bratunac. He was the platoon commander of the Slapasnica Unit within the Bratunac Territorial Defence. He was mobilised into the Territorial Defence in March 1992. Then he was assigned to the reserve force of the police station in Bratunac. He observed that at this time, there were more Muslims than Serbs in the police force. In April 1992, Mr. Vujadin Stevic was ordered to organise night watches in his village, Slapasnica, which was surrounded by Muslim populated villages. At night he often heard shooting above the Muslim villages and was aware that armed conflict was imminent. He knew that his leader had tried every means to avoid the war and tried to reach a peaceful agreement with the Muslims, but the Muslims did not agree. The Serbs were very frightened after some Muslims at the SDA elections realised -- rallies expressed hatred against the Serbs. On around 2nd or 3rd May, 1992, Vujadin Stevic heard that Muslims in Hranca had attacked the JNA column as it was withdrawing from Central Bosnia and many were killed that time. On May the 8th, 1992, Vujadin Stevic received news that the Muslims in Srebrenica had ambushed and killed paramilitary deputy and the Judge Goran Zekic and wounded a number of Serbs. This was confirmed at a later meeting in Territorial Defence headquarter in Bratunac. He was given task to go to Glogova a with unit whilst received strict orders not to kill anyone unless they were attacked. A while later, Vujadin Stevic was told by a soldier that they followed a Muslim to a shelter and found a pistol on him. At the shelter, they found a homemade explosive device, and there were around another 200 Muslims in the nearby woods. Vujadin Stevic did not take any pistol from the -- from Musan Talovic, because the pistol was found by his soldiers. He also never called Najdan Mladjenovic over the radio, and he did not receive any orders from him to kill the Muslims. In around June or July 1992, he was assigned to the army of Slapasnica and then moved to Pajici and Cizmici. A few days later the Muslims attacked Pajici, setting fire on it and killing or wounding many civilians. After that a company was formed which was commanded by Milivoje Stjepanovic from Slapasnica. And that would be the short summary. At the moment I do not have any questions for Mr. Stevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stevic.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In fact, you were an active member of the SDS. In fact, you were a candidate of the SDS at the first multi-party election for the Bratunac municipality Assembly in November 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a president of the SDS local board in Slapasnica, I was a member of the Municipal Board of Bratunac, and I was a candidate on the list for deputies in the Bratunac Municipal Assembly. However, I was not among the first 24 who made up a joint Assembly in Bratunac. Only after the Muslims walked out of the Assembly I was elected to the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you were also member of the Serbian Municipal Assembly from the very first session in December 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you didn't mention this in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think that that was necessary, but it's beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received an interpretation that he was a member of the Serbian Municipal Board, but it says the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. A Municipal Board can also mean a political party board.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: What I meant was the municipal -- the Serbian Municipal Assembly, not the party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Municipal Assembly. You said it correctly, but the witness is receiving wrong interpretation. So it's the Municipal Assembly, and it was said a local commune. It might affect the witness's answers and his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, do you confirm that you were a member of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Stevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but after the Muslim population had left Bratunac. Mr. President, if I could have the volume turned on, Mr. President, because I'm hard of hearing a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope you are now hearing better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, if you could kindly come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you better. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Costi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have Exhibit P03199, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the Serb Municipal Assembly of Bratunac from 1991, 1992, and 1993, and as you can see from the page 1 in the English version and page 2 in the B/C/S version, you're listed among the members, number 27. It's actually probably page 3 of the B/C/S. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 in English, and it will be page 6 in B/C/S, now we see the minutes of the 13th of February, 1992, session, and on the following page, the English is halfway through, page 4 in the B/C/S, it's again halfway through the page, you'll see that you took the floor at that session. So is it true, isn't it, that at least in February 1992 you attended the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac meetings?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that this is a minutes of the meeting of the Serbian Assembly. It is perhaps a meeting of the SDS board in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: You said it at page 3 in the English version, the minutes of the first regular session of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. In any event, we can move on with you. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my name in the last line, but the sentence is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We probably need the page before for the B/C/S at this point, which is page 6, where the minutes of that day begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we go to the prior page of the B/C/S, please. Here we are. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We can see the date and the heading.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can see the date. Mr. Prosecutor, this was a long time ago, and I don't have particular recollection of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. Now, on the 8th of May, you were tasked together with your unit, the TO unit from Slapasnica, to take part to the Glogova operation to take place the day after; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. My village is bordering Glogova, and an order was issued for them to carry an operation of disarming in Glogova, and I was requested to reinforce my defence line between Slapasnica and Glogova, and I acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, during the operation when you were walking towards the centre of Glogova, you captured a group of 20 Muslims that were hiding in some kind of a shelter. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't capture them personally. It was done by my fighters. Of course, following an order from our superior. We had to go down to the centre of Glogova so that we wouldn't have to go back through very forbidding terrain. On the way, they came across a number of Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes, and it is in your statement. Now, you soon after join your unit who had captured these 20 men and you walk them to Glogova, to the market or the shopping centre in Glogova. When you got there, you ordered them to stand against the wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, while we were waiting for our superior to come and tell us what to do. At the same time, I provided protection for them from any possible problems that might occur. I told them to stand against the wall so that would protect them from that side, and on the other side we provided protection pending the arrival of our superior who would possibly question them about what was happening in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, I would ask you -- we'll get there, to just try to focus on the question that I'm answering you -- the question that I'm asking you. Now, you ordered the men to stand against the wall and also to face the wall and to keep their hands up; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this Court has heard the evidence of one of these 20 men, Musan Talovic, that you also cite in your statement, and at P3188, which is a statement, he said at paragraph 25: "When we arrived to the village, it was 10.00 in the morning. Stevic told us to line up against a wall and face the wall at the supermarket." And later on in the same paragraph: "They also ordered us to put our hands up." You ordered them to put their hands up and to face the wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct. First they stood against the wall, and then I told them to sit down. But, please, once again I said here that there were about 20 men. Nobody counted those people. It may have been 15 of them or fewer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, there were actually 23 in fact. Anyway, contrary to what you stayed in your statement at paragraph 22, it was Najdan Mladjenovic who told you to bring these prisoners to the market because they were actually commanding the TOs in this specific operation. Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not know Najdan Mladjenovic at all. It was impossible for him to contact us on the radio that was carried by our superior in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now can I have 65 ter 24845.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, this is an article published on the Balkan investigative reporting network web site, and it discusses the trial that is currently ongoing before the Bosnian state court in Sarajevo, and it's the -- it's the Mladjenovic case. It's a trial about the crimes in Hranca and Glogova, and halfway through the page it says, the paragraph that begins "on," it says: "'On May 3, 1992, Mladjenovic carried out and took part in the attack on the village of Hranca in which several Bosniak civilians were imprisoned and killed, and whose houses, under his orders, were burned down. Also, he commanded over the attack on the village of Glogova six days later, when he issued the order that 20 Bosniak men from that village be killed,' said the Prosecutor, emphasising that there were underage children among the killed." Now, I'm asking you again Mladjenovic was commanding the TOs in Glogova and ordered you to kill these 20 men. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and he didn't come to me. I didn't know him. Later on, I heard in 1993 or, in fact, he was wounded in 1992, but in 1993 when my unit established a communication line between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, the food warehouse was in his house and that was when we first met. He originated from Hranca, and I don't know which activities he was involved in. Our units were completely separate, and there was no significance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me tell you what Musan Talovic, one of the 20 men, stated here, and it is again P3188, paragraph 24: "Stevic contacted the Vojvoda, a man called -- contacted a Vojvoda, a man called Najdan Mladjenovic, through his radio. I knew him before the war. He lived about 2 kilometres from my house. We could hear the conversation and Stevic asked Vojvoda what to do with the 23 Balijas. Vojvoda told him to bring us to the centre of Glogova in front of the supermarket." And then at paragraph 31: "The Vojvoda ordered Dragan to execute the rest of us. He said to Dragan, 'Executioner of the punishment, get done with your work.'" Is it true, isn't it, Mr. Mladjenovic that -- Mr. Stevic, that Mr. Mladjenovic ordered you to execute these prisoner and that your nickname is Dragan?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: The nickname of Dragan is actually not a nickname. It is my Christian name. My official name is Vujadin Stevic. I tell you once again: Mr. Talovic can write whatever he wants. It's not true. My superior was one of the JNA active duty officers and the purpose of the operation was to secure the road in order to have certain forces of the JNA withdrawn from Central Bosnia. Given the fact that there had been an incident a few days previous in Hranca village, that is why some measures were taken, i.e., another attempt was made to disarm the Muslims. I have to say that the Muslims in Glogova had built shelters so that they can take cover easily after an operation of theirs or after they had set up an ambush along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript. The witness said, "I say again that Mr. Musanovic," that is line 9 -- no, "Musan Talovic," not "Mladjenovic," that he could write what he wants. If we listen to the transcript, we'll see that he said that Musan Talovic could write what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you didn't know Mladjenovic at that time, but I would say that you knew it very well. He was a TO like you in 1992, and you were both member of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 00603F. And if we go to English page 2 and B/C/S 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: At that session there was a discussion about reviving the local boards of the SDS and both you and Mladjenovic were tasked to revive local board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the interpretation. Could it please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, if you read the second conclusion -- or the first conclusion -- let me check. The second conclusion, which is at page 2, and is also the second conclusion at page 2 of the B/C/S, it says: "To revive the work of the local board in Fakovici, people in charge of it are Nedjo Nikolic, Zoran Tesic, and Miroslav Deronjic. Vujadin Stevic is in charge of the local board in Slapasnica. Dragan Radic is in charge of the local board of Borici. Milo Vasic and Najdan Mladjenovic are in charge of the local board in Repovac." So as you can see from here we are both cited in the same paragraph one session of the SDS Municipal Board tasked with similar mission and goals, and so what I would say is that you knew each other, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, we did attend the meeting together, but I was never in any close contact with that man. There may have been over 20 or 30 people there. Now, why would I have any need to be friends with anyone in particular? Hranca village is some 14 kilometres away from my village. I couldn't know everyone, especially because before that I had spent three days working in Western Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Those people -- three years working in Western Berlin, and the people there changed a lot over that time. I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript. Those young people grew up while he was in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So let me close on the Glogova operation. Now, you know that the person you captured were killed, and you probably know that 40 others were also killed, and I'm sure you know that the village was burned down, and the rest of the population was expelled. I'm asking you: The goal of the operation was not to collect weapons, but it was to expel Muslims.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with your assertion. The number of killed that day cannot be based solely on the statement of a witness. In the records of Bratunac municipality, there is precise information on who was killed when, on what date, with their first and last name, their personal numbers, et cetera. Such lists drafted by someone with the aim of increasing the number, well, on such lists you can even find people who had previously died or been killed, even those who had never been born. The only truthful document is the register of citizens because that is where the families reported the names of their family members and the dates of their disappearance or when they were killed. Anything else is not credible. Could we please rely only on such records as the true documents. I do know that the late Miroslav Deronjic had agreed to accepting this increased number of the killed, and the names were gathered from who knows where and many -- I don't even have their date of birth or their personal number. In my view, it is terrible to find that a Tribunal of this sort would use such random data without relying on credible documents. I don't want to waste anyone's time, but in Republika Srpska I can tell you that every tree that is cut down in the forest receives its number, and it is precisely known what household cut it down, where it is, and in which part of the forest, let alone information about people. I personally believe that it is terrible to make a list of -- as this of first and last names without appropriate personal information, such arbitrary lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's move on to -- to the following days. The day after, on the 10th of May, you said in your statement that you participated in another operation. You were tasked with blocking Mihaljevici because another operation was ongoing. Now, is it true, isn't, that that morning Mihaljevici was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Mihaljevici was not torched. None of the villages below Bratunac was in the direction of Zvornik. They were not set fire to, not a single building, but there was an operation with the goal of disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, this -- this Tribunal, this Chamber has heard the evidence of a protected Witness which is KDZ605, and in his statement at paragraph 45, he discussed and said that at 9.00 a.m., Mihaljevici had already been ablaze. Do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Interpreter, it is not Mihajlovici but Mihaljevici. Perhaps a haystack had been set afire so that this would be a signal to start with the process of disarming. But definitely no building was set on fire all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the following day, and at this point I think we are around 11 of May, you were tasked to find Muslim hiding in the woods, and you explained at paragraph 26 and 28 that you did find a group of Muslims and that you organised their transportation to Bratunac. Now, what I don't see in your statement is that these persons, these Muslims that you organised the transfer of, were forced to do so, they had no alternative. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: You are not, Mr. Prosecutor. It did not take place on the 11th. I cannot be precise, but it was a few days later, perhaps on the 13th or the 14th or even the 15th of May. That is when I was informed by my people that a group of neighbours in Radjici [phoen] settlement which was part of Mihajlevici village along the road between the Ljubovija bridge to Zvornik, that is to say at the place where the road crosses the Drina, they sent a man to call me to arrange with me how to leave that territory safely. Of course, I met their request. I remember well that I came to a house. In a room they were praying, and with my left arm I motioned them to continue, and in the room to the right I saw my schoolmate Hajrudin Dubicic. Since I knew him best I approached him, greeted him, and we started talking about the problems and what was going on. They were in fear. They did not dare be next to the road, because different paramilitary formations moved along the road, firing in the air and causing fear. When the people praying in the other room finished their prayer, they approached us. We knew each other from passing quite well, although not necessarily by first and last name. We sat down and tried to agree on what would be the best thing to do. Out of fear they did not wish to be in their homes, and they could no longer be in the forest. They wanted to leave their village because they were eyewitnesses. They could see that all women and children from the Serb villages had crossed the bridge over the Drina and left for Serbia. It wasn't safe for them either, and they felt fear, especially because there was chaos everywhere in the town itself and in the villages as well. We agreed that I would contact my superior in order to try and secure transport. That is how it was. I secured their transport to Bratunac. I did tell them that those were still up in the forest should come down, too, so that it would all be in one go. They came the next day, and I know that they couldn't fit in one bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It is in your statement, Mr. Stevic.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: -- and that it had to go back two or three times. Very well. And that's how they left the village. They were grateful, especially certain individuals who told me that they fared well, that they managed to leave Bratunac without being mistreated, and up to this day people come back to me with stories like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That part is already in your statement, so sorry to interrupt you, but the time is very short. Now, when you said in your statement that they reached Bratunac without problems, now, you didn't say in your statement, though, what was happening in Bratunac to the Muslims that were captured in the surrounding villages, meaning most of them, families detained at the football stadium, and men mistreated and killed at the Vuk Karadzic school. So they might have been safe in Bratunac, but in Bratunac they actually encountered pretty serious problem. Isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: These people definitely not, because they confirmed it to me after the war when they returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. But you know that thousands of Muslims were detained in Bratunac and at the Vuk Karadzic school men were mistreated, tortured, and killed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I know of some stories, but I had no occasion to see it. You know that in my village at the time, the telephone lines were down. I could only rely on a radio device which had a direct connection with the TO staff. I wasn't informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24843, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this is an article that was published on the 5th of May, 2010, on a Bosnian news web site and is about Milenko Prodanovic also known as Mungos. Milenko Prodanovic, the article discuss some of the crime he committed in Suha and particularly the killing of a pregnant woman, and then in the second page of the article both in English and B/C/S, there is a bit an interview, part of an interview of Sakib Ahmetovic who is the -- was at least in 2010 the president of the Association of Detainees in Bratunac, and he says: "'I was imprisoned by Milenko Prodanovic and taken to the camp by a man who introduced himself as Chetniks Vojvoda Dragan Stevic. Everyone called him Dragan, however his name is Vujadin Stevic,' said Sakib Ahmetovic, president of the association of the camp inmates." You can find the full interview on the internet of the federation TV web site. Now, isn't it true that you actually escorted prisoners to the Vuk Karadzic school, so you were fully aware of what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this really begs a story, and I apologise for taking up time. Mr. Sakib Ahmetovic was a good neighbour of mine. After the war, when I again became president of the local commune in Slapasnica where the village in question belonged to, he had an argument with his neighbour Sahman - I don't remember the last name - concerning a path and a fence. They called me to the spot as the local commune president. When the surveyor and the municipal inspector ascertained the border between their two plots, then he and Sahman his neighbour, I don't remember his last name, but they had a fight. I simply didn't want to get involved. And it seemed funny at the time because I had saved both of them from those - how should I call them? - people who caused disorder at the beginning the war and yet now they were fighting, and instead of being grateful that I testified in court in his favour rather than Sahman's. When the criminal report was dealt with, he put this up on the internet, and it just seemed ridiculous, because on the internet you can put whatever you like. That was the reason why he wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, thanks for that lengthy explanation. At this point I have very limited time. I'm going to move to 1995, the events that follow the fall of Srebrenica. I have just two question for you on that. First of all, you said that -- well, at that time you were assistant commander for logistic in the 1st Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, and on the 12th of July you said that your battalion captured in Cizmici a group of the UNPROFOR soldiers, and then you brought them to the Hotel Fontana where they were detained by the army. Now, I don't need you to retell me the story that's in your statement, I would like you to just answer yes or no to this question: What you did was against the will of the UNPROFOR soldiers. They were arrested against their will. They were not free to leave. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: You are not. If I'm allowed to explain, I'd be happy to. Otherwise, you can take it whichever way you like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, I take it the way that's in the statement, which is -- which you just confirmed is sort of voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now can I have 65 ter 06202.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: This is a Security Council, United Nations Security Council, Resolution 1004 on 12 July 1995, and as you -- we can see in the middle of the page, it says "Condemning." "Condemning the offensive by the Bosnian Serb forces against the safe area of Srebrenica, and in particular the detention by the Bosnian Serb forces of the UNPROFOR personnel." And in the following page the Security Council: "Demands the Bosnian Serb forces to immediately and unconditionally release unharmed all detained UNPROFOR personnel." So it seems like the United Nations had a slightly different view from yours. It appears that they were forcibly detained. They were detained, and they asked for their release.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Please, it would be the same as if I were to say that you detained me and sent me to the hotel room to sit down and wait until it is my turn to testify. They were all invited to come to the hotel to take shelter from everything that was going on there, as people under UN protection. And I only see the humane side in it all and nothing bad on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Maybe on your part, but you are aware that the VRS then threatened to kill these UNPROFOR soldiers if the NATO bombing had not stopped. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was being arranged up there at the command, but I do know that there was bombing in the area of Bratunac and Srebrenica. So this is incorrect too. No one did it out of fear. We simply acted in the most humane way by escorting them to the hotel, you see, because at the time no one guarded them with any rifles. No one guarded them at all. It was just the police who walked up and down the street, and people waved from the windows. I see nothing in it all save for the humane gesture. I have to say this: When I arrived at that place, we waited for this young man who could speak English, I think it's in the statement, and when I established contact with an UNPROFOR fighter, he told me, he showed me the trench where only two days before there were 500 armed Muslim soldiers. So how do you explain to him that -- whether UNPROFOR had done what it had been sent to the protected area of Srebrenica to do in the first place? And he said, "Thank God you hadn't arrived here earlier, because all of those Muslims would have been killed." I even want to say this: I responsibly claim that I still see some of those guys that I -- well, if I were in contact with them, I believe they would be delighted now to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, last questions. At paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A quick question. What did you mean, Mr. Stevic, by an UNPROFOR fighter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the soldiers of UNPROFOR. I just used the wrong word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 36, you said in your statement that in the following days before being deployed to Zepa, you remained at the battalion command in Magasici. But this is not true, is it? You were actually deployed together with your battalion looking for Muslims that were left behind the column, Muslims that were still hiding in the woods. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. You're not correct yet once again. When my commander sent me to escort UNPROFOR soldiers, he told me when you hand them over to the brigade in the hotel, I should go back to my tasks in the battalion command at Magasici. And my tasks were to organise food and possibly the replenishment of ammunition for my men on the line. It lasted for a day or two, and then we went to Zepa. I -- there was no need for me to chase the Muslims who were there. There were some other units who did that. My unit was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02114, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: This, Mr. Stevic, is an order from the command of the Bratunac Brigade to your battalion, and if we read at point 1, it says: "The 1st Infantry Battalion will search the terrain of the former enclave of Srebrenica on the right side ...," and then it goes on indicating the three points and the villages of responsibility of your battalion. And this was issued according to the order of the Drina Corps command, which is D02239, just for the record. So your battalion was actually tasked with searching the terrain or chasing the Muslims, as you said, on the 14th of July, and this was its occupation until the 17th when, as you said in your statement, you were deployed to Zepa; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the order. Perhaps the commander was familiar with it. However, my battalion could not move either leftward or rightward. It could only advance a bit forward through the woods, and eventually they returned even before they reached Srebrenica. It returned to Magasici, and perhaps one or two days later we packed our belongings and we went to Zepa from there. Let me repeat once again my personal task was at the command of this Infantry Battalion in Magasici. I was there to secure the command and make sure that there was food. I was in charge of the rest of the logistics tasks for the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have this document admitted, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So to conclude, Mr. Stevic, you were in Magasici during those days. Now, the Chamber had the opportunity to visit those areas, but just to remind ourselves, Magasici is on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, and if I'm correct it's let's say halfway between Kravica and Bratunac, around Glogova, a little bit southern than Glogova. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: It is on Avdagina Njive. It is an elevation, and to the left you can see Magasici if you're looking from Bratunac towards Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you know that at the time you said you were there, on the 13th of July a thousand -- over a thousand of Muslim men were killed at the Kravica warehouse, and you know -- which is about 5 kilometres from your command, and you probably also know that in the following days the bodies of these thousand men were buried in Glogova, which is, I would say, not even a kilometre from your command. So were you aware at that time that execution were taking place and that the bodies were buried, I would even say, in your backyard almost?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Please, once again you are using wrong numbers. At the beginning of my testimony, I said that it is really sad that the number of dead and killed is being distorted and blown up. All these men have their names and family names, and all the other details, and I'm sorry that you measured them like you would cubic metres of stone or wood. Nobody really knows the exact number of those who may have been there. Those who gathered them and brought them there did not count head. I'm particularly insulted by the numbers. Kravica was not in my area of responsibility. It was to the right of my area of responsibility if you're looking from Magasici towards Srebrenica, and it was approximately -- or, rather, it was -- it was part of the responsibility of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade that was attached to us. To the right in the direction of Konjevic Polje, the command of the brigade left a corridor at the moment when the line was established between this 6th Battalion of Zvornik and the military brigade. So all the Muslims could leave, i.e., they could go. They did use that corridor but not to leave but to go to Tuzla to fetch weapons to increase their weaponry which is another sign that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, the question was whether you knew the executions were taking place and bodies were buried. Did you know or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know. I did not have the time to deal with that. If something happened behind our backs, there was no way for us to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you do not know the executions were going on, on what basis can you say that the number is being distorted?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If I may follow up. What would be the right number?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I said at the beginning when we started talking about Glogova, you go to the municipal records to find out the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are now talking about Kravica warehouse in 1995. You said you didn't know that but you also said the number was being distorted, and even you said you were insulted. How come? Could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm insulted by the arbitrary numbers that are being presented here. If something happened, then the exact number should be known. All the dead people deserve to be identified, counted, and buried. Only such information containing the first name, the last name, or the exact number, but as I've been following these trials for a year, nobody mentioned the same number and nobody actually used the proper information about those casualties and victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stevic, I'm asking you again, what is in your view the correct number of people killed at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know the right number, but I know for a fact that it was much lower. You have access to all the information. At least you have an opportunity to access information in Bratunac and Srebrenica. That's where the families of the victims are, and they personally reported who was killed, on what day, and in which place, and this is the only kind of information that I accept as credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We did access this information. We did have exhumation. Did exhumation. We have numbers. The numbers are the one I said. What is the basis for you to say that it was a lower number? You don't know.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I claim that because you did not use the official records. You used the lists of some associations which are arbitrary, just like the list of Musan Talovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think I have any other questions, Your Honour. I forgot on my way through to seek the admission of three 65 ter numbers which were: 24845 and 24843, the two articles, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go one by one. The first one seems to be the article published in -- on an internet web site which contains the Prosecutor's opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the probative value would it have at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it doesn't itself. The only value would be to have it on the record to -- when assessing the weight of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was read to the witness and there's no need to admit it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The second one would be 24843, but I believe probably the same thing applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 24sata --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: 843 which is the other article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we object. The witness didn't confirm anything about it and it has no probative value as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The witness gave a long explanation as why the article and why that witness said those things in that interview. So I believe in this case the witness provided a sufficient basis for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it an interview, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It was a report, and the last bit, the one that I put to the witness, is part of an interview where a witness was talking about being brought to the Vuk Karadzic by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it so that we can see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure. It is 2 -- here we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like you in the future to deal with it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm very sorry. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understood you are not tendering at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It is my mistake. I completely overseen this. It's in the second page. The second paragraph -- sorry, the second from the bottom. And this is a statement from Sakib Ahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you first tell me what this document is about and what this web site is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, the web site is a -- is a Bosnian news general web site. It reports news on the Balkans, and this particular article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is 24sata?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah. That's the name of the web site. And the article, though, it's about an interview, a video interview that was taken by the federal television during which Prodanovic refuses to answer the question and he sort of almost violently reacted to the journalist. And because of this interaction between the FTV journalist and Prodanovic the -- was quite violent, it reached the news, and this is the news about that interaction and that interview. And in the web site, there is also a video which we didn't upload because we didn't think it was worth to upload the actual video of Ahmetovic interview which is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given that the witness offered a very lengthy answer, statement, with respect to this bit, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And the last one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: UN Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah, but that one, we've already, I think, admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And the last one is 0 -- sorry. It's 00603F, which are the minutes of the SDS Municipal Board that we discussed at the beginning of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the relevant part of the document, which is 65 ter number 603. So only --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: 603F, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A couple of questions, perhaps three, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stevic, were you known to people as a Chetnik Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: The first one who referred to me as Chetnik Vojvoda after the war was comrade Ahmed Husic, my colleague. I thanked him for the title that reached me from the enemy side or the opposition side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Topalovic's statement he says that somebody communicated with Vojvoda Mladjenovic, was Mladjenovic a Chetnik Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know none of us were Vojvoda and that includes him, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause before you start answering the question for the benefit of the interpreters. Do you understand that? And the line 6, "Topalovic" should read "Talovic." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was my mistake -- my mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a nickname as a fighter?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I had several nicknames. As I've already told you, my real name is Vujadin. Dragan is the name that I was christened as. During the war they called me Tito, Cica, and many other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tito would not be a Chetnik nickname, would it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't, but things happen, don't they.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you learn about the incidents in Kravica at the farm there?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: As we were leaving for Zepa, we passed by the warehouse. We could not see anything in front of it. We were in vehicles, so I could not see anything in front of the facility. And as for what was happening inside, we could not see that from our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you familiar with the warehouse? Can you tell us how large is it? How many people could fit in there?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there are two or three buildings there, and those are mostly buildings for farming purposes. I did not measure them. I don't know what their surface is. I don't know what their volume is, so I wouldn't dare speculate, but they were enough to serve the purposes of one village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now my last question: You were asked about the Serbian municipality of Bratunac. Why was it called the Serbian municipality? Was there any other municipality? Had there been an agreement with this regard?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN STEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Serbian authorities and the Muslim authorities in Bratunac had tried to agree how to avoid war and how all of us could stay in that area. The Serbian police was thus formed in order to control the Serbs, and as far as I know the Serbian police abandoned the police building and only the Muslim police stayed there. There were also talks about organising both the Serbian and Muslim municipalities in order to avoid a conflict happening in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 17, the witness didn't say "to protect the Serbs" but the Serbian police was to control the Serbs and the Muslim police was to control the Muslims. This is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you listen to the tape, I'm sure that you will see that I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Stevic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Mr. Stevic, that concludes your evidence in this case. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If I could have one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. Then you may be excused, Mr. Stevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. During my cross-examination of Jovan Nikolic on 14 of March, I played a video which was admitted as P06202, an interview with Mr. Karadzic where he's claiming there were mass executions or executions at all, and the Trial Chamber and the Defence asked me for the date of that interview with CNN by Mr. Karadzic, and for the record, the date was 28 November 1995. I sent a link to Mr. Robinson yesterday which has the transcript of that CNN interview with Mr. Karadzic. We've uploaded that to show the date as 65 ter 24847, and we can either make it part of the video exhibit or stipulate to the date or whichever the Trial Chamber prefers. But the date, I think, is beyond dispute was 28 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, did you have any observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I hadn't seen this or had any -- had notice that this was going to be offered as an exhibit. I'd like to take a minute and read it, it's four pages long, and get back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not include that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And no objection to redacting it so that it matches the video part. It's just -- I just want to make the date clear for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember properly, in that footage I wear very light clothes, and it was on the 28th November. In our neck of the woods, it's very cold at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I take it Mr. Robinson will come back to us. Given that we -- the Chamber has a meeting, we will have a break for 35 minutes and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obradovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Obradovic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just like in case of everybody else who speaks Serbian, I would kindly ask you to pause between starting your answer after my question and to try and speak as slowly as possible so that everything can be recorded. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D7973 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I have read it many times, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation to be complete and I ask you to do the same. Can we please now look at the last page so that you can confirm if that is your signature, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect everything that you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They would be completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement and 92 ter package into evidence. There's a document mentioned in paragraph 12. I would like to lead the witness live on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can you help us with respect to associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're offering 13 associated exhibits. Nine of them are not on our 65 ter list because we didn't have them at the time that the list was submitted. We would ask that they be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. As we indicate in our e-mail last night, we object to the admission of the three photographs referenced at paragraph 7. That's 65 ter 1D12075 through to 1D12077. These documents don't meet the standard for associated exhibits in our submission. It's not even indicated in the statement that the witness has recognised these photographs as being what they are meant to -- depicting what they are meant to depict. In addition, there are markings on the photograph, and there's no mention in the statement that these markings even exist let alone who made them or what they are intended to depict. And I note also that there is B/C/S text on some of the photos that's not translated. So in our submission these photos would have to be led live to be admitted. We had indicated that we were objecting to the last sentence of paragraph 12 because it describes a document that hadn't been identified. I've just been informed of a 65 ter number that that is -- sentence is supposed to refer to, and as Dr. Karadzic mentioned, he's intending to deal with that document live, so we'll reserve our objection to that sentence for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to agreeing with Ms. Gustafson's submission, I also draw your attention to the document, i.e., 1D7300, which is referred to paragraph 19. The Chamber doesn't consider that that document forms an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. It is just simply listed at the end of the paragraph. So except for those four documents, we'll admit the statement as well as the remaining nine associated exhibits. Shall we give the number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement will be Exhibit D3175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the remaining associated exhibits will be given numbers by the registrar in due course. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read the summary of Mr. Obradovic's statement in English, and after that we are going to deal with some documents that we intend to offer. [In English] Dragomir Obradovic was born on 27th of June, 1950, in Krsevi, Sokolac municipality. He was the commander of SJB Sokolac and a member of the Crisis Staff of Sokolac municipality in some months in 1992. After the constituent Assembly of the SDS party was held on Sokolac in August 1990, the first multi-party elections were held. The SDS won the elections, but afterwards there was a distribution of power, and many key posts in the government went to Muslims. From 1991 onwards, there was growing mistrust among the population, often increased by the media in BH. While there were no open confrontations between employees at the police station, there was considerable disunity between Serbs and Muslims. Through operatives in the state security, Dragomir Obradovic learned that Muslims were arming and forming paramilitary units and preparing to set up Muslim police station in the areas where Muslims were a majority. Mevludin Smajic, a high-ranking official of the MUP has admitted that he brought weapons and explosives to the Muslim -- Muslims and organised training in making explosive devices. In one case, on 21st of July, 1992, Muslims launched an attack on a house in village without provocation using mostly automatic rifles and a hand-held launcher grenade. The Serbs fled the village. When the JNA mobilised in June 1991, Serbs responded to the call-up while Muslims boycotted it at the instruction of the SDA. During this period, the police force had a special unit intended to -- for rapid intervention in major disturbances. This unit, however, began without authorisation to carry out actions that contravened the regulations that were in force at that time. Mr. Dragan Obradovic immediately proposed to the Crisis Staff that the unit be disbanded, which happened. There were no paramilitary units in the municipality. The Crisis Staff passed a requiring any sighting of such group to be reported. No reports were received. The police took all measures to preserve security throughout the municipality. As soon as the Crisis Staff was formed, it called the representatives of all parties to participate in joint actions to preserve peace. However, this move was condemned by local Muslims, and the SDA did not attend. The Crisis Staff was required to make -- to take measure -- measures such as restricting the work of catering establishments and prohibiting the movement of armed individuals in public places in order to preserve public law and order. No fighting from took -- took place in the municipality until the second half of 1992. On 27th of July, 1992, Muslims blocked a Serbian village, arrested some civilians, and took them to a camp in Zenica. Several days later, another attack on Serbs took place in the village of Donje Babine, and in August another attack was carried out on the village of Cvrcici. Following these and other attacks, Serbs pressured police to disarm Muslims in certain areas -- in certain villages. Dragomir Obradovic and his colleagues visited the Muslim village of Pedise to collect illegally-possessed weapons, but when the police patrol arrived to collect them, the villages -- villagers had left rather than hand over their weaponry. After the attack -- an attack on a Serb village on 21st of July, 1992, Muslims who had organised the attack left their villages. The entire population of Mangurici, Sahbegovici, and Meljine left instead of handing their -- over their weapons. This showed that Muslims were not forced to leave but did so voluntary. In Vrhbarje, for example, Muslims lived peacefully until October 1994 when they moved to Sarajevo. Muslims were killed by police units in the Novoseoci and Arbinjska Propast. The Sokolac police station took no part in this, and the civilian authorities were not informed. In all cases where the police became aware of killings, proper procedure was followed, investigations were carried out, and a criminal report filed. The police did not set up check-points along any roads, nor did they control the movements of Muslims. Occasionally police patrols were put up, but only when the police were aware that the perpetrators of specific crimes were in the area. Despite the conditions of war, the police continuously carried out their regular tasks. There was never a prison at the police station. Individuals could be detained no longer than 48 hours or, in exceptional cases, 72 hours. Those who were detained were properly fed and nobody was physically punished. Dragomir Obradovic has no information regarding the military detention unit established in Sokolac. Local mosques were destroyed, but the police were not informed about this. It was apparently done by local residents because it was believed that the weapons were being kept there. And that is short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a brief summary of your statement. Now I would like to ask you to help us shed some light on a number of documents. Do you have a hard copy of your statement, or if you don't -- actually, could you ask the Chamber for permission to use it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please be allowed to use my statement in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have it with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 you speak about the freedom of movement, and you said that you saw a document that speaks about that issue. I'm talking about the freedom of return. Had you known that even before the document was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that the Crisis Staff decided that all the people who had left the territory can return without any impediment provided they had no weapons on them that could be used in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have now 1D4355 in e-court. Unfortunately, it hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the people start leaving Sokolac municipality, and members of which ethnic communities left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After the Serbs left Sarajevo, towards the end of 1992, the Muslims from this area started leaving it so that they headed towards Sarajevo because there were already available facilities where they could find accommodation. This was done by the villagers of Tocionik, Kalimanici, and those on the edges of Sokolac municipality who had committed certain crimes as mentioned in the statement, i.e., the killings of the villagers of the aforementioned villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say that the Serbs left Sarajevo towards the end of 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Late 1991 and early 1992, and also some people left after that date if they managed to do that with the aid of UNPROFOR and other agencies involved in exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at this document dated 23rd of April, 1992. It speaks about the conclusions reached by the Crisis Staff of the Sokolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 in your statement, but on the screen you can see the document that deals with this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the first paragraph say? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff who invited the people who had left Sokolac municipality to come back and that their security would be guaranteed provided they do not bring any weapons with them. That was the conclusion adopted by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that all the people who had temporarily left the territory of the municipality to return home without any fear for their personal safety and the safety of their property because there were no reasons for their moving out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a public proclamation which was broadcast on Radio Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, before you start answering the question, please put a pause for the benefit of us who are relying on the interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I just have a minute of your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 2, read it, and then tell us what it speaks about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the witness is reading the paragraph, perhaps he could read it out loud for the benefit of the non-B/C/S speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we zoom in a bit further. Mr. Obradovic, could you read it aloud, para-2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Presidents of local communes and other activists in local communes shall maintain constant contact with representatives of the legal authorities in the area of municipality. All the possible problems shall be resolved through legal institutions of the government system in the area of municipality in order to ensure the functioning of the authorities in the entire territory of the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now read paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "It has been estimated that so far in the area of municipality there had been no incidents involving citizens of various ethnic backgrounds and that all the organs should carry out continuous actions in order to maintain and preserve the situation, good neighbourly inter-ethnic relations." I'm sorry, I have the wrong pair of glasses, and this is not big enough for me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you leave your glasses somewhere in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but obviously they are not suitable for reading from the computer screen. They are good for reading from paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "President of the local communes bordering with the areas of other municipalities shall contact with the relevant organs in the municipality and inform them of any incidents of attempts by incursions by -- attempts of incursions by individuals and organised groups or any other formations in the area of municipality which might cause anxiety among the citizens and disturb peace in the area and subsequently they shall inform the Sokolac --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause yourself as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I have to keep reminding myself of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 7, the first sentence please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "To enable regular supply of basic necessities and food to all inhabitants of the local communes and" -- I don't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just slow down and put a pause. And if the interpreters could speak to the microphone. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does to mean to enable regular supply of food to the inhabitants of all local communes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that at the beginning of the war there were certain products that there were insufficient quantities of, a decision was made that all inhabitants should be supplied with such products that could be found in the shops. In the villages and hamlets Muslims, too, received such products that were in short supply, things like flour, sugar, salt, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you directly participate in terms of your position in organising visits to those local communes, and what was the aim of such visits?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Our station area was divided in five security sectors. Each sector was headed by its leader who daily visited their sectors, touring villages and talking to people. At the end of the day, the policeman in question would draft an official report once he returned from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the name of the person who attended this task the longest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: All of the policemen did their work depending on the needs of the service. Sometimes they stayed even after their working hours. The sector leaders were both Serbs and Muslims, so if there was any need, the policeman who was on duty that day would sometimes be required to stay all the way up until midnight if necessary and if required by the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mentioned -- do you mention the name of Rade Dubovina anywhere in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Rade Dubovina lived in Polje. He was 30 or 40 years of age at the time. He was in charge of being in contact with the inhabitants of Novoseoci and to supply them with products and whatever was necessary. He was also tasked with co-operating with the policeman in charge of that part of the area in terms of assigning -- or making arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to read out what Witness Munira Selmanovic had to say about it which is on page 18553 and 554. She says: [In English] "Nobody was going anywhere. People were working until the 1st of May. On the 1st of May we were given holidays. They said we would summon you back to work. Nobody went anywhere. And as I told you, these people were stopping by, Macar, Savic, Velimir, all of those people came as well as Rade Dubovina, who used to come by practically every day --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you stop there. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
