utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I don't think it's appropriate for Dr. Karadzic to read out the evidence of another witness to have this witness comment on it. If he wants to make submissions later about what various witnesses said about someone that's fine, but he can just ask the questions in an open way and elicit the answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I disagree with that completely. I think it's helpful to the Chamber and very fair for Dr. Karadzic to put to a witness what another witness has said, quoting directly is even the best way to do that, and it's open to the witness to make any comment. There's nothing leading about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes Mr. Karadzic. Do you have anything to add to what Mr. Robinson already said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just to say that the Prosecution only recently quoted the words of another Prosecutor to a witness, that is to say from another proceedings, and I am talking about witness who spoke here confirming the story that this witness has to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, would you like to respond, or could you expand why it would be inappropriate to put the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, my response to Dr. Karadzic's comment would be there's a difference between a direct examination and a cross-examination, and in cross-examination it's a given that you put evidence in the form of document or witness evidence to the witness and that's -- that's the nature of cross-examination. So the analogy is inapposite. As Dr. Karadzic said, he wants this witness to confirm what another witness said. I just don't see the point in that. As I said, if he wants to make submissions later about the fact that witnesses were consistent on a point that's fine, but he can just -- he just should elicit the evidence and later make those submissions, and asking this witness whether what someone else said is consistent with his evidence is of no benefit to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Gustafson, while we understand your point of distinction between the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, but in this case having led some foundational questions, the Chamber does not see any difficulty with putting such questions. He could have it -- he could have put it in a more neutral way, but we don't see any difficulty with it. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll read this out in English so as to receive appropriate interpretation. "[In English] And as I told you, these people were stopping by, Macar, Savic, Velimir, all of those people came as well as Rade Dubovina, who used to come by practically every day, and he would be talking to people, People, there is no need, it's like this, like that. I told you everything."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the position was of the authorities concerning potential departures of people from Novoseoci or other villages? Were the authorities in favour of their departure or were they trying to talk them out of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities tried to keep everyone in our area, and they were trying to talk them out of moving out. They wanted fuel so that they could leave, and the Crisis Staff of the municipality did provide it so that they could continue with their sowing and harvesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on page 18549 and 550, this lady said that they went to the municipal building asking that they be evacuated and the authorities talked them out of it saying that there was no reason to leave and that they should freely go home and would be provided with everything that they need. Now that you mention fuel, I'll read something out from page 18556. It had to do with whether these were the Sokolac authorities. "[In English] All of them are from Sokolac. First Savic, then Milorad Savic, and this other persons said all right, come with us, buy fuel, work with machines, buy what you need, all of that is correct. Then they would come to some village, bring whatever was needed, people would take that. There you go, that's how it was. These were these favours done by the people of Sokolac." [Interpretation] How does this tally with your knowledge concerning the position of the authorities concerning the Muslim inhabitants in the Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The overall authorities treated all of the citizens equally. There was no distinction made. If someone needed assistance, they were helped irrespective of whether they were Serb or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think this goes too far, and it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Obradovic, how did it happen that you preserved peace in Sokolac municipality until late July, that is to say, four months after the outbreak of war in all of the adjacent municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: We preserved our area for four months so as to avoid war. Had it not been for the murders in the border areas of the municipality, we would have awaited the end of the war without fighting each other. However, the murders provided a spark which set off all of the further clashes. The inhabitants of the village asked the police and the army to protect them. I know that even women stood guard with their children around their homes while the men were engaged in the 206th and the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. So a poet of ours said that in wounds human blood turns bad, which means that once the bloodshed started, it was simply an incentive to fan the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for the interpreters with translating "njegos" [phoen]. It should actually say that human blood makes for very bad food.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this admitted for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean this one, 1D4355.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, the photographs of the initial firing at Serb houses. Who took those photographs and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The police, that is to say the crime police which carried out the on-site investigation. They took the photographs on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As part of their investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can now those photographs be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us take a look at those photos one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D12075, 6, and 7, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you said in your statement and in your testimony, there had been no clashes before that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you explain to us what is depicted in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko Batinic's house in Donje Babine. When Mr. Batinic died, the Serbs came out on the third morning as was customary, and upon returning from the cemetery at noon that day, the people sat down to have lunch. However, Muslims opened fire from infantry weapons, and they even used a mortar. They tried to have the shell land in through the window. By sheer chance or luck it struck underneath the window, and we see the shards of glass and pieces of stone which flew around wounding many around the house. Later that night, all of the Serbs fled Donje Babine to Knezina where they stayed until the end of the war. The next morning, the Muslims left, too, because they probably didn't dare any longer following that kind of incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the meaning of the circle in the right-hand side corner? Can you read what it says in it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The place where a shell hit. This is where a shell hit, the black spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see the following photo, 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you read out the title of this photo. Shall we scroll up. Could you read it out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slowly, and can you articulate, please. This has to be recorded. It has to be translated for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "Slavko Batinic's house which was attacked by Muslims on the 31st of July, 1992, and where Serb civilians were shelled."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what this is, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This is a house on which fire was opened. I don't know who the house belongs to. It doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it be the same house but the photo was taken from the other side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the other side. That's where -- where fire from firearms was opened on it from automatic rifles, whereas a shell hit the other side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we see the following page. 77. Who was in charge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The lawyers of the crime investigating police, whereas the police officers secured the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out that aloud which is written together with an arrow. Do you see "Mjesto" something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Shell impact location."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the picture depicting the same house as the one we saw for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house is depicted from the front and from the eastern side, I suppose, where fire was opened on it from automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's when the house was full. There was a festive dinner taking place.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some 40 people inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3186 through to Exhibit D3188 respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, due to your decision I'm not going to insist on the clip from Vrhbarje. That village lived in peace all the time. They hugged each other when they said their good-byes, but it is proof that the authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is just commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No submission. So I take it you are not tendering 1D7300. Is that what you're saying, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if this is your decision. If on the contrary your decision is to lead the witness live, I would very much like to show that clip. I didn't understand you properly. I thought it was unacceptable, but it may be acceptable if it is led live. So can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the document, please? The number is 1D7300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see whether it's relevant and admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Muslims continued to live in villages around Sokolac and in which villages, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Give me a time reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the start of war up to a certain moment in time, for as long as they say.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Novoseoci, Vrhbarje, Micivode, Kuti, Knezina, Kaljina, Sahbegovici, and Meljine. These are the villages where Muslims went on living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the document and tell us whether it is correct that it was only on the 31st of October that Muslims from Vrhbarje requested to move out from the village? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims of Vrhbarje remained there until 1994. They were there throughout the war living there. They co-operated well with the locals of Zovjedovac [phoen], Vitomira [phoen], and Sarci [phoen], and they really looked after each other. I was present when people be requested to be allowed to leave the area. That was allowed to them eventually. I was there when they greeted each other. Both the Muslims and the Serbs cried. They hugged each other. People then got into their cars and they simply left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a film by the Norwegian television channel about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are the one who drafted this document; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report that I sent to the MUP to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document is saying that 61 Muslim civilians were removed. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, well. These are translations for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They went of their own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking the witness. Could you read out the document, the main text. Could you read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in a little. "On the 29th of October, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 29 of October, 1994 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot possibly follow the speed of the witness's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness is reading the main text. Could you start again, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 29th of October, 1994, at 1300 hours, a relocation exercise was carried out from the village of Vrhbarje, municipality of Sokolac. A total of 61 persons of Muslim ethnicity moved out. This was organised by the commissariat for exchanges of Republika Srpska. The policemen from the public security station in Sokolac handed over the aforementioned persons to the KP Dom in Kula and accompanied that hand-over with certificates. There were no other elements over the past ten days that would have had an impact on the security situation as per the order of the President of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the objection, but actually I am grateful to you for having noticed in -- the mistakes in the translation. This will be the main issue that the Defence is going to raise, the accuracy and the correctness of the words in translations. I have no further questions. Has this document been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Obradovic, as you have noted, your evidence in -- evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, that is through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: A few moments ago you were looking at some photos, I'm sure you recall, of Slavko Batinic's house, and you said that the crime police took these photos on the spot as part of their investigation. That was at page 50. Was that investigation -- did that investigation take place shortly after this incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That happened sometime around 1300 hours. I can't be more precise than that. I don't have those documents. That was reported to the police. The police went to the site and carried out an on-site investigation on that same day as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to 1D12076, which I think has been admitted as D3187.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is one of the photographs you looked at a few moments ago that you said was taken by the crime police as part of this on-site investigation on the same day as this incident. Now, in front of the house, in the bottom right-hand corner of this photograph, you can see some snow on the ground; is that right, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: There was no snow. The land was dry. I don't know whether this is snow or what. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That white patch on the ground, you can't conclude that that's snow? Do you have any idea what else that could be other than snow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to the next one, 1D12077.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Obradovic, in the foreground in front of this house there is snow on the ground, and to the left of the house in the trees somewhat behind the house you can also see snow on the ground in the trees, can't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The photo is true. I don't know what else to say, but there was no snow.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, clearly these photographs were not taken by the crime police on the 31st of July when this incident took place; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, because the police went to the location to take photos of the house and to carry out an on-site investigation on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But these photos can't be those photos, right, because these photos have snow in them, and those photos were taken on the 31st of July. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At paragraph 1 of your statement, you said that when the war began, you were the commander of the traffic police station and then later you became the SJB commander. At what date, to the best of your recollection, did you become the SJB commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I believe that that was after all the turmoil that happened. After the Muslims left Sokolac municipality, I became the SJB commander. I was appointed by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document we saw a few moments ago from October 1992, I believe, indicated that you were the SJB commander. So you were at least by October the SJB commander. Do you remember how long before that you had been the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Before that period I was an SJB commander from 1986.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I think you're maybe confused with your position as the traffic police station commander. I'll just move on. At paragraph 28 of your statement that you said that due to the dismissal of some Serb police in Stari Grad, Zoran Kitic, the SJB chief, asked the Muslim policemen from Sokolac not to come to work any more until this issue was resolved. In fact, Mr. Obradovic, on the 23rd of March, 1992, the Muslim employees of the Sokolac police station and the traffic police station were simply dismissed, and you were involved in informing members of the traffic police, Muslim traffic police officers, of that fact; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that I did something in Stari Grad. As far as I can remember, you stated that at the beginning of that sentence. However, I did not have any authority over the police station in Stari Grad. The Muslims in the Stari Grad police station dismissed all the Serb policemen and only Rade Tusija [phoen] remained. After that, Zoran Cvijetic, who was the chief of the police station, invited all of the Muslim police in Sokolac to come to a meeting and he told them that for as long as the staff issues were unresolved in Stari Grad that they should not be returning to work. All the police officers kept their personal weapons, I mean pistols or short-barrelled weapons, and after that I sat down with all those Muslim police officers in our mess. We -- I bought them drinks and coffees. There was -- there were no harsh words said among us. Nobody was angry. I wished them a lot of luck, and I said that I hoped that they would soon come back to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P6089.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I could ask you, Mr. Obradovic, because my time is very limited, if you could try to focus your answers as much as possible on the precise question that I am asking, and I will try to keep my questions precise. Now, this document is a SRBiH MUP record of statements.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Can this be zoomed in a little?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm actually going to direct your attention to the next page. This is what some Muslim police officers from Pale and Sokolac said at the time about what had happened in their police stations. And if we could go to the bottom of the second page. It refers to a statement by Mahir Caldarevic. Can you confirm that he was a member of the traffic police in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Again can this be zoomed in a little?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, it says that this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mahir Caldarevic said on the 24th of March that on the 23rd he had gone to the traffic safety police station in Sokolac and the commander had told him that the Crisis Staff of Sokolac municipality and the government of the Romanija SAO had decided to remove all policemen of Muslim nationality from work. Now, you were the commander of the traffic police station at the time, so I'm assuming this is a reference to you. Can you confirm that this is what you told Mahir Caldarevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was not me. It was the chief of the police station, Zoran Cvijetic, who said that, and this person, Mahir Caldarevic, the name doesn't ring any bells. I don't know of any policemen bearing that name. Caldarevic? Mahir Caldarevic. Is it a mistake or something? Mahir Caldarevic, the name doesn't ring a bell as somebody who was affiliated with the police station ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 24848.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 28 you also said that the Muslim -- even after the Muslim policemen stopped working it be SJB they continued to receive their salaries.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of war activities, of war operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This document is MUP list of employees who performed duties at this place station referring to the Sokolac police station in April 1992 and received a salary advance for the month.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in -- perhaps we could just go to the B/C/S. Thank you. And zoom in on these names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now this list of employees who received a salary for April 1992, they're all Serbs; right? There are names on the next page I'd like you to look at as well. Are you looking at the document, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes. Look, these are salaries for April. At the beginning of April war started, so they were no longer on our public security station's payroll after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I just add something? Zdravko Krstic had arrived from Sarajevo and joined our station. People came from Sarajevo to fill the places that those other people abandoned. The war had already started then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 9, Mr. Obradovic, you referred to the Special Police Unit in Sokolac. Was that the unit led by Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Not Dusko Malovic. It was Pera Suka.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were there two Special Police units in Sokolac, because the Chamber has also received evidence of a Special Police Unit from Sokolac led by Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Pera Suka was a commander of this unit. Dusko Malovic's name was mentioned in some context, and I think he worked at the MUP at the time. That's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 15 of your statement, you said that it was after events at the end of July and early August, these attacks that you referred to, that the Serbs began pressuring the police and the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade to disarm Muslim villages, but in fact the Bosnian Serb forces began disarming Muslim villages well before the end of July 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. There were only attempts at reaching an agreement. When the army started, that's when the fighting started. Again, before that I went to the village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed the issue of weapons. I told them that they could hand over the weapons for this. They didn't have any permits, whereas if they had permits they could keep them. All of them claimed not to have any weapons in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You answered my question right at the beginning, so I don't need all this detail at the moment. If I need details, I'll follow up with additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P5242, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a -- these are the minutes of a Crisis Staff -- a Sokolac Crisis Staff meeting held on the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S, to item 16. And it's at the bottom of the page. If we could make it as large as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Item 16 says: "Drago Macar informed those present that the plans for disarming certain villages were made. It was concluded that the decision on the aforementioned shall be made later." Now, Drago Macar was the TO commander at the time and then he became a commander in the VRS when it was formed in late May, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And he actually died soon after this meeting. On the 2nd of June, 1992, he was killed when his vehicle hit a mine; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the front in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. And that was on the 2nd of June or thereabouts; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. I cannot recall any specific date.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Karadzic already referred to the evidence of Munira Selmanovic from Novoseoci. She testified that in the spring of 1992, Drago Macar came to her village and asked the men to hand in their weapons and they handed over some weapons, and that's P3295, paragraph 3. And in her testimony, she specified that this took place around the 27th of May. That's transcript page 18551. And she also said she knew Drago Macar as he was from the neighbouring village. So it's clear given that Drago Macar was dead around the 2nd of June that Muslim villages began to be disarmed well before late July; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Drago Macar was the neighbour of those people down there in the village, and most probably he talked to them because they started arming themselves extensively. He as a commander may have initiated some action on his own, but in view of the fact that he was the commander, I'm not in a position to comment on what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. At paragraph 20 you discuss later events in Novoseoci, and you said that approximately 40 Muslims from that village were killed after the civilians from Novoseoci had been evacuated to Sarajevo, and that this suggests, Mr. Obradovic, that those who were killed were not civilians. But in fact what happened was the soldiers came to the village. They separated out every able bodied male from the village, and that included a 15-year-old boy, an 82-year-old man, as well as a number of men in their 60s and 70s, and I refer to P3297 for those facts, and they killed them; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that 40 men were killed and that that was done by members of the military. I don't know what the cause of that was. I personally condemned that incident and as did all the municipal officials. We thought that to be a heinous act and an operation which blemished the reputation of the municipality of Sokolac. Later on I heard some stories to the effect that five of our men in Kaljina came across an antitank mine and got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That information is in your statement so I'm just going to move on to my next question. And you also said in your statement that the civilians from Novoseoci were evacuated to Sarajevo. In fact, the women and children were simply ordered onto buses and taken to Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't present on the spot. Somebody did that, but I don't know how. Most probably this is the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you also asserted in your statement that before this killing the Crisis Staff had allowed the villagers to organise armed guard duty during the night. However, the Chamber has received evidence that the authorities disarmed this village. Ms. Selmanovic's evidence that I referred to earlier about Drago Macar's disarming the village in May and P3296, which is the 2nd Romanija Brigade's record of the confiscation of weapons on the 27th of July, 1992. So whatever theoretical permission they may have had from the Crisis Staff to organise armed guard duty to protect themselves would be useless if their weapons had been taken away; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Weapons can be confiscated, but they can easily obtained again. Once they were taken away, new ones would be obtained. And once the war started, people were in possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16 can we add what witness said at the end of the sentence. He said, "I don't know." [In English] "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your statement you were informed about the killing of the Muslims from Novoseoci on the 22nd of September, the day it happened, that evening. How did you hear about this? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who told me. I just heard the news that these people were killed, but I don't know who I heard it from. Since that was a military matter, we did not interfere with that nor did we include any police forces in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you heard the news. So was this more or less general knowledge in the -- in the area by the evening that -- on the day that this killing took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you couldn't remember who exactly told you. You just heard the news. So my question is was this common knowledge in the area that these men had been killed by the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness say he heard the news or he was informed of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He said, "I don't know exactly who told me. I just heard the news that these people were killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was looking at the statement. My apologies. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, did you understand the question? Was this something that people were generally talking about by the evening of the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I think it's clear from your answers, but if you could just confirm the police didn't conduct any investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Police did not conduct any investigation because that was beyond our jurisdiction. It was performed by the military police and the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the military police and the Military Court didn't investigate either though, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, do you know, because you lived there at the time, that these victims bodies were only exhumed in the year 2000? That's P3297.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that since in 1993 I was working in Bijeljina. I wasn't aware of the details of this incident nine months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but you agree that if a proper investigation had been conducted at the time, these bodies would have been exhumed and examined right away; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Calls for speculation even of medical nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. This witness was a police commander at the time. I think he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can you answer the question, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That if a proper investigation had been conducted by the military authorities at the time, the bodies of the victims would have been exhumed and identified right away, not in the year 2000; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but nobody conducted exhumations in other places as well. Nobody was involved in this kind of activity. But, yes, you are right. If everything had been done properly, that would have been a different case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, please, in the transcript, his answer said that not even Serb bodies were exhumed at the time. That is what the witness said, that not even the Serbs were involved in being exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have 65 ter 24854, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, before the break you had said at page 67 that the military police and Military Court investigated the Novoseoci killings, and then when I put it to you that they didn't investigate either, you said, "I don't know about that." So I'd just like to show you this document which is a report of the 23rd of September, 1992, from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade commander, then Colonel Krstic, to the Main Staff, and at item 1.C, which is a little bit further down the page, it says: "In the villages that were recently...," "ciscenje," translated as "mopped up or cleansed," "... namely Kuti, Micivode, and Novoseoci, the remaining parts of groups managed to withdraw in some places." And the Chamber has already received a report from Krstic of the previous day describing the events in Novoseoci in very similar terms. That's P5438. Now, there is no indication in this report that an investigation into the events in Novoseoci is being conducted or even that a crime has occurred. Colonel Krstic describes what happened in Novoseoci in rather standard military terms, or, sorry, as a standard military operation, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm a little late with this, but I'm going to object because all the witness is being asked to do is say what's in the document. He's not -- there's no indication that there was an investigation from this document, and, you know, what the document describes, so I don't believe that the witness can add anything by answering that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I asked him that -- I put it to him that the events were being described in standard military terms. I think that's a real question that can be answered. And in any event, it's still a question that goes to impeachment of this witness in terms of his evidence about a subsequent investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I see here is an attempt to get into evidence a document that shouldn't be gotten into evidence through this witness, so I don't think that it's proper to put up a document for which there is no connection to the witness and ask him something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I could easily ask the question another way. He's asserted that there has been an investigation. I could say, "Did you know that Colonel Krstic described the operation in Novoseoci in this manner the day after?" If the Chamber prefers, I could ask the question that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that I did not intervene on page 67. The witness did not say that the military police investigated this. He only said that this was beyond the jurisdiction of the regular police, but he never confirmed that the investigation had been conducted by the military police, and that was not recorded in the transcript. Nevertheless, this has been taken as the foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, you can re-examine on that if you think it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 67, the witness said police did not conduct any investigation because that was beyond our jurisdiction. And further, the witness said, it was performed by the military police and the Military Court. Do you remember having said that, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that that should have been done by the military police and the Military Court, should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber prefers the formulation you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, did you know that the day after the killings in Novoseoci Colonel Krstic described what had happened there as mopping up or cleansing to his commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: How can I know that? Krstic did not submit any reports to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Really, Mr. President, this is a real unfairness to allow a document to be admitted into evidence this way when a witness knows nothing about it, is expected to know nothing about it. It doesn't contradict or confirm anything that he would be expected to know or has said in his testimony. And especially given that General Krstic refuses to testify in this case, it's really unfair to allow this to be considered as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the document is very straightforward, and the purpose for which it's being admitted is simply what Colonel Krstic reported the next day. I mean, it's right there in black and white. Unless there are any authenticity concerns, which I hear none, this document is completely admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it is a separate matter whether this document can be admitted through a bar table motion with certain requirements, but the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation. We'll not admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 24854, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This, I think, has been admitted as an associated exhibit as D3180.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you said that the police didn't investigate this crime because it was beyond your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you've maybe given the wrong number, because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She's given us the exhibit number. You gave the 65 ter number of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. Yes, this is the document I want, D3180.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you referenced this document in your statement at paragraph 22, and you say that it confirmed that you took all legally prescribed measures against individuals who in any way disturbed public law and order and regularly filed criminal reports against such individuals. Now, this document states that the Sokolac SJB had filed four criminal reports against VRS members and had brought misdemeanour proceedings against another ten VRS members, if we go to the next page. Oh, sorry, we've only got the one language. So, Mr. Obradovic, it's clear that you brought charges against VRS members in this instance. You could have done the same for Novoseoci; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not the same thing. These people against whom reports and criminal reports were filed were not in uniforms, but they were members. They spent a fortnight on the line and then took a rest for two weeks. When they went to town they did not wear uniforms, and for that reason reports were filed against them as civilians, in actual fact they were members of the military, but they committed these felonies and misdemeanors whilst in civilian clothes and proper reports were filed against them accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this: The day that this crime was committed you heard about it informally. You said you can't even remember who told you, but you heard the news. So this was clearly informal information that you had that the perpetrators of this crime were VRS members, and you certainly couldn't have been sure at that point that there were no civilian perpetrators among them. What you could have and should have done is investigated this crime, and if your investigation determined -- confirmed that the perpetrators were VRS members, then you should have arrested them and handed them over to the military authorities for prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is your question relating to this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: What is it relating to? I didn't understand your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll ask it again. The day this crime was committed you heard the news that it was VRS members who committed this crime. So this was informal information that you had. You're a police officer. If you had received such information at the time, what you could have and should have done is gone immediately to investigate what happened, and if your investigation had confirmed that these perpetrators were VRS members, at that point you should have handed this over to the military police; right? You shouldn't have just sat there and done nothing when you heard about this horrible crime taking place in your municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The area of military responsibility was the zone where the army was. They had military courts and military police, and wherever members of the military cause problems it was a matter to be dealt with by the army, not by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another topic. If I could have 65 ter 24734, please. Now, at paragraph 19 you talked about the villagers of Vrhbarje who you say moved to Sarajevo of their own freewill in October 1994. Now, by this time, by 1994, there very few Muslims left living in Sokolac municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, this is a statement of a man named Avdija Katica from Vrhbarje. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember his face, but I knew quite a few people of that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They were from Vrhbarje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we move down to the third and fourth paragraph in this page. It starts about the middle of the page. Mr. Katica talks about what happens prior to this moving out in October, and he explains that in July 1992, Serb neighbours including Ilinka Saric and Drago Djokic -- oh, sorry, my mistake, in this capacity he talks about how the villagers handed in at least most of their weapons to the 2nd Romanija Brigade in July 1992. Can you confirm that this village was disarmed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they surrendered their weapons. If they did, that means that they were disarmed. But it was never difficult to procure weapons. I may hand in a rifle today and have a new one the next day. So people used to bring weapons with them, for example, from Sarajevo, and distribute them overnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to page 2 in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, this is still on page 1 in the B/C/S, at the bottom. Mr. Katica talks about how Serb neighbours, including Ilinka Saric and Drago Djokic, from Dzedovci [phoen] made it possible for them to survive by assisting them in trading their agricultural products, and in your statement you said you were surprised at the level of care that existed between the Vrhbarje villagers and Serbs in neighbouring villages. Is this the kind of care you were talking about, the Serbs were helping them trade their products?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Even today if I cannot sell my cattle, I will look for someone who can do that for me. That's what they did throughout the war. If they needed to sell something, they would look for a person who can arrange that for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the next page in the B/C/S, and this is at pages 2 to 3 of the English. Mr. Katica describes how on the 17th of April, 1994, nine men from the village were taken to the 2nd Romanija Brigade Commander Krstic and from there they were sent to work on the front line fortifying positions and digging trenches, et cetera, and after 15 days they were allowed to return to the village for two days, then they were taken out again in 15 to 20-day shifts with two day rest periods in between, and this continued until the 30th of July 1994. Were you aware that the men from this village were being taken to the front line to work in the spring and summer of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know. I do know that there were working groups where Serbs participated too, those who did not join the army be it because they refused to or were not mobilised. There were so many Serbs in Sarajevo who dug so many trenches across Mojmilo Polje and elsewhere and yet no one asks about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said I did know that there were working groups where Serbs participated too. So you were aware that there were working groups where Muslims were working. For the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say Muslim. I know that there were Serbs who volunteered to do so, but I have no knowledge about this matter regarding Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then if we go to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I truly ask that it be interpreted as it should. The witness said that Krstic -- I don't know about Krstic mobilising them. This is way too free in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness speak loudly, clearly, without mumbling, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, the interpreters have asked that you speak more loudly and clearly to assist in their interpretation. Thank you. If we could go to page -- stay on page 2 of the B/C/S. On the bottom half of the page, Mr. Katica talks about cattle being looted from their village at night throughout 1994 and an incident on the 16th of August, 1994, when mass thieves looted their houses and hit one of the villagers with a rifle butt, and this incident caused the villagers to start spending the night in the woods. Were you aware of these kinds of incidents in the village or the fact that these villagers had started to spend the night in the woods out of fear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It is incorrect that they spent their night in the forest. I am aware of this detail because I was present when it took place. Namely, during the day two or three criminals arrived. A person sold a horse and received 400 German marks and they took the money from him. The people from Vrhbarje went to see Sarac, a neighbour, because they were afraid. I was in the field in Sokolovici. They called me and myself and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- went to see this Sarac in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dovar [phoen] Sarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And could you start over from there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did you go with? That's the name they didn't pick up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please wait for the end of interpretation. We didn't hear it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't hear you because you spoke while they interpreted Mr. Karadzic's words. So who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milovan Zuban, deputy commander of the station in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. It's still not clear, Mr. Obradovic, how you can confirm that these villagers didn't start spending the night in the woods after this event. You weren't in that village every night to confirm where they were at night, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to finish, to explain. Namely, having arrived in the village to Mr. Sarac, there were 60 people, women and children included, were seated in the house. When I asked them what had happened, they explained that Hamo -- that someone had taken -- had hit Hamo and took 400 German marks from him. He suffered lightly bodily injuries, and policeman Zuban took him to Podromanija, to the military hospital. He was administered help and his bruise was taken care of. He had a cut. I tried to have the woman who saw it describe the person involved to me. She started describing, and in the meantime someone else asked me something. When I turned round and when I responded and turned back, the woman had gone. No one else wished to provide any statements. That evening, I called another two policemen. We returned them home. We put each of them in their house, and I left policemen to guard them that day and the next several nights because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you are speaking too fast again. "We put each of them in the house and I left policemen to guard them that day and the next several nights because they were afraid." Please repeat what you said after that, slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After you what have just read? Of course, there were criminal groups who went to villages. They even came to my mother who was alone in the village at the time, but no one ran, and I guaranteed every evening that they would receive a policeman if necessary so that one or two policemen would guard the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you said you left policemen there to guard them that day and the next several nights. So after that, you don't know what happened at night in that village, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After that I think I provided policemen for five or six days to secure the village, and after that I had no reports of anyone attacking them in that village. It was a coincidence. It could have happened to any Serb. It happened that people came, took money, those criminal groups that were later caught, and reports were submitted against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Then at the bottom of this page and at the top of the next page Mr. Katica describes how a man by the name of Djurkovic, the Municipal Assembly secretary, came to the village on the 10th of October, 1994, to speak with the villagers about their intentions, and Mr. Katica said that if the authorities could not guarantee their safety, then they should be allowed to go to Sarajevo. And then other officials came to the village to discuss the conditions of their departure, including municipal president Milan Tupajic. Now, was this transfer arranged by the civilian authorities as described here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They asked to go. I don't know what they discussed with Tupajic or with that man, the other one that is mentioned. I only know when they were supposed to go we went there as the police to provide security so that everything would end safely in terms of their departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So although you assert that they left of their freewill, you have no knowledge of their discussion with the civilian authorities who arranged their transfer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge. No one invited me to those talks, and I can't discuss something that I was not present at.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, Mr. Katica states that on the 29th of October, 1994, they were bused out of the village escorted by a policeman named Ivan Sarac, and instead of going to Sarajevo for exchange as they had been told, they were taken to Kula prison. Now, earlier in your testimony today you said that these people got into their cars and simply left, and that was at page 55. However, they were, in fact, taken under police escort to Kula prison; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They were taken by bus. I didn't say vehicles. I think some international community representatives were present there. They were taken to Kula. I don't know what happened next. Kula is right next to the border near Sarajevo. The border passed by Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Kula is a prison; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Kula is a settlement, and there's a prison at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They were taken to Kula prison, weren't they, Mr. Obradovic, escorted by the Sokolac police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They were take to the Kula location where there is a prison. The police returned from Kula. Now, what else did the authorities do later on is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at something you do know or you did know at the time, and that's at D3189, and again this is a document that's referenced in your statement and that you actually looked at earlier today. This is your document signed by you that says that on the 29th of October, 1994, the day Mr. Katica confirms they were moved out, 61 Muslim civilians were removed from the village of Vrhbarje. The next sentence says: "They were turned over by policemen of the Sokolac police station to the Kula penal and correctional facility with a receipt." I'm going to ask you again, Mr. Obradovic. These people were taken to Kula prison escorted by the Sokolac police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The exchange commission was present, too, and it was stated that they were to be taken to Kula. How should I know what was done later on? It's mentioned that there was this Commission for Exchange. They should have taken care of it. Even if they were taken to Kula, again they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, it's a very simple question. You're not answering it. I'm going to move on. You make assertions about fighting that occurred in other villages, villages which you claim were armed with all kinds of infantry weapons, and that's at paragraph 30. Now, the Chamber received evidence from a witness who saw one of those villages, Meljine, being shelled by tanks and howitzers and burning, and that's P131, page 9. Did you actually witness the attack on this village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know these villages were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that operation was carried out by the army. I couldn't even get near there. It was within their remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 25 of your statement you said that a military detention facility was set up in the primary school in Sokolac, and it was there for ten days or so --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, Your Honours. I intended to tender Mr. Katica's statement. I should have done that before I moved on to the next topic. That's 65 ter 24734.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you're going to -- we object to the admission of this statement, but if you are going to admit some parts of it, we think you have to be very careful in admitting only those parts that were confirmed or contradicted by the witness. There are a couple of -- there's a paragraph on page 2. I have to call this document up in front of me again but -- I can give you more specifics, but there's a paragraph on page 2 that I think can -- was confirmed by the witness concerning the care that was taken for their -- people in their village, and I believe there was a paragraph on page 3 that was confirmed by the witness concerning thieves that came and looted from them, and then on page 4 concerning their transportation to Kula prison there was a paragraph. So I think that those three paragraphs were confirmed or contradicted testimony of the witness, but there's a lot of other information in the statement that has nothing to do with anything that was even asked of the witness and some things that the witness didn't confirm. So if you are going to admit a third-party statement made three years after the event to law enforcement, then I would think it has to be very limited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the witness certainly confirmed various aspects of the statement and indeed the entire statement does contradict the witness's assertion that these people went to Sarajevo of their own free will. The thrust of the statement is quite the contrary, so I think that coupled with the fact that aspects of this statement were confirmed and indeed corroborated exactly with the -- the documents -- the document that was admitted through this witness, I believe it meets the standard for the admission of these types of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the witness's answer that he was present when it took place, the Chamber is of the view it can admit the document in its entirety. It's only three pages. Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, at paragraph 25 you said that there was a military detention facility set up in the primary school in Sokolac and it was only there for ten days or so when it is relocated to the primary school in Cavarine at the beginning of October. Now, you said it was a military detention facility. Was this facility under the authority of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: What was under whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The military detection facility that you state was set up at the primary school in Sokolac and then was relocated to the primary school in Cavarine.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was only in operation at the primary school for about ten days or so. Can I ask you what the source of your information is for that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I simply heard of it. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your sentence. Could you repeat your sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was some kind of detention for a few days at the school and that it was later moved to Cavarine. I never went there, and I don't know what the conditions there were and what sort of thing was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber's received evidence that that detention facility in the primary school in Sokolac was in operation from July 1992 until October 1992. So a lot longer than ten days. Now I take it based on the fact that you never went there and you only heard about this that you can't exclude the possibility that you are wrong about the dates during which this facility operated at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was for a short time only. After some time it was used to receive Serb refugees who came from Sarajevo and other places. Even Muslims from Sarajevo came there. There was a woman with her two children who was accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you can't be sure that it was only in operation for ten days. It could have been in operation for longer than that prior to October -- or, sorry, prior to September 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say whether it worked for five or ten days. I don't know any exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm putting it to you that it was in operation for a lot longer than that, several months. Can you exclude that possibility or should we go through the documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long it operated. I don't know exactly. I know that refugees came after that and that they were placed at the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraphs 23 and 24, you discuss the detention of people at the Sokolac SJB, including Becir Homarac who was from Micivode, a neighbouring village of yours. This was someone that you knew. Now you said -- now after his detention at the SJB, he was sent to the military detention facility at Cavarine; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Not that it was closed -- that he was detained, but he was held when he was interviewed by members of the state security. Then he was sent to that detention there, because he had nowhere to return. Those villages had been cleansed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. The Prosecutor said detention, and the witness received interpretation that he was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how much of a difference that makes, but that's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So at paragraph 23 of your statement you said that after people had been held at the Sokolac SJB, the person would either be released or referred to the prosecutor for further action. It's clear from your answer just now that Mr. Homarac was neither released nor referred to the prosecutor. He was sent to detention at Cavarine. So that was a third option, wasn't it. They were either released, referred to the prosecutor, or they were sent to military detention; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was sent to Cavarine for an exchange because in Micivode, his village, there were no more people. I can't return him to Micivode to walk around the village alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you assert that it was for his own safety that he was sent to a military prison instead of being allowed to go home; is that correct, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He couldn't return home because there were no people up there. He would have remained alone, and for security reasons he was to be evenings changed. That's how Serbs were exchanged from Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to go to one last topic and document, it's 65 ter 01110. Now, Mr. Obradovic, Mr. Milan Tupajic was the president of the Sokolac municipality during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is Mr. Tupajic's answer to a telegram sent from Dr. Karadzic to various municipality presidents, including him. It's D95. And that telegram had placed responsibility on municipal presidents to ensure the protection of Muslims and Croats who hand over their weapons and do not intend to fight. Now, you can see here that Mr. Tupajic states several things in response. First of all, he says that the headquarters of the TO has not existed since the 21st of May, 1992. Now, that's a reflection of the fact that the Sokolac TO had been incorporated into the VRS at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the 2nd Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And he says that the chief of the SJB had submitted his resignation. Is that correct? Did the chief of the SJB submit his resignation sometime in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he submitted his resignation or whether he was removed. His name was Rado Birac.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But he left his position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. If you want me to explain, the man is a writer, a poet. He joined the station and all of the problems that happened. He thought that he could deal with them slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't think we need that level of detail at the moment. Now, Mr. Tupajic, at the end of this message says that the protection of the local Muslim population has to be taken by the 2nd Romanija Brigade and the SJB. Now, those were the two organs in Sokolac at the time with primary responsibility for security matters; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think I heard you agree, but I didn't hear an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you just repeat your answer, please, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Those two organs deal with security in the territory of a municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, could you come closer to the microphone. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the end of this message Mr. Tupajic says: "In conditions as they are now, I cannot take responsibility for their safety." Now, it's correct, is it not, that the president of the municipality was not anywhere in the chain of command of the Sokolac SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And similarly, he was not in the chain of command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender this document and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This witness can't speak to this document at all. He can -- there -- you know, he can identify certain organs that are mentioned in the document. This is a subterfuge, you know, to have the Prosecution admit through a witness who can't speak to a document evidence that will reflect on Mr. Karadzic's knowledge, notice, things like that that should have been put through a witness who could speak to those issues, not to smuggle them in through another witness who can only say that, "Yes the MUP was working at this time," or "The TO was not working," and then to use that as some kind of pretext to admit the document. So we think that on balance the prejudicial effect of admitting a document in this manner would outweigh any probative value that you might get from admitting given this witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There is no subterfuge here. I think this -- I mean, the witness has confirmed virtually every aspect of the document. He's confirmed the position of the author, the date of incorporation of the TO into the VRS, the fact that the chief of the public security station had left his job, the organs responsible for security and Mr. Tupajic's position or not in the chain of authority of those organs. I mean, this -- every aspect of this document has been confirmed. These documents are admitted as a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber agrees with Ms. Gustafson. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the document is on the screen, could you please first tell us: Besides physical security, could the municipality do anything else for the citizens including Muslims, and did it do something for them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever the citizens of the municipality needed they got from the municipality to the extent of the municipality's abilities to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether on the 14th of July it was confirmed that the measures of disarming Muslims were not implemented in the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is in relation to a question that was put to you during cross-examination. Allegedly what Macar collected from his neighbours was considered official disarming. Before mid-July, were there any efforts to disarm Muslims officially?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened before mid-July. Macar talked to his neighbours, but they did not surrender their weapons at the time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us display another document. Let us see what was handed over in that village. Let's look at D1667. You have already told us that it was not difficult to obtain weapons, but let us look at this report and let us see what the army had to say about that. D1667. The command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps sent this on the 27th of July, 1992. At the end -- or, rather, in the second half of the passage, Novoseoci village, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
